examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Write the quantifier scope explicitly and state whether the domain is nonempty. To negate a formula, move negation inward one quantifier at a time, switching universal and existential quantifiers. To disprove a universal claim, one counterexample suffices; to refute an existential claim, exclude every witness. ‘Exactly one’ requires existence and a separate uniqueness condition.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
On domain {1,2,3}, how many functions f satisfy ∀x∃y (f(y)=x)?

**Answer: 6.** The formula says every domain value is attained, so f is surjective. A surjection from a finite three-element set to itself is a bijection. There are 3!=6 such functions.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
The witnesses y may depend on x. Replacing ∀x∃y by ∃y∀x would require one input to map to three different outputs and is impossible here.

Do not interchange universal and existential quantifiers without proving equivalence.
